author.bio: I lead the content team at Dynamic Dreamz, shaping clear, purposeful narratives across blogs, landing pages, and brand communication. With a strong grasp of SEO, storytelling, and buyer intent, I focus on creating content that’s not just readable but also useful, relevant, and built to drive real business outcomes.

children: The question of Shopify Metafields vs Metaobjects is quite persistent because people most often get confused about which one they should use. So let us provide you with more detailed info on that.

Both metafields and metaobjects let you add custom data to your Shopify store, but if you choose the wrong one, it can be quite problematic: duplicated content that’s painful to update, or unnecessary complexity for something simple. So, let us have a practical way to tell them apart, but let’s get started with the core difference between them.

Metafields attach extra data to something that already exists: a product, a page, a collection. Metaobjects are standalone. They don’t belong to anything by default; they exist independently and can be referenced from multiple places at once.
The simplest way to remember it: metafields extend a resource. Metaobjects define a new one.

Use a metafield when the data is specific to one resource and isn’t shared anywhere else, even if the same value happens to appear elsewhere. Two products might both weigh 2kg, but that’s a coincidence, not a shared object.

content: Material composition, care instructions, technical specs, warranty terms
A unique field on a single landing page that won’t be reused

children: If you’re only ever entering a value once, for one thing, a metafield is usually the right call.
Use a metaobject when the same content needs to appear in multiple places, and updating it once should update it everywhere.

content: A brand story block that appears across several product pages. With metafields, updating it means editing every product individually. With a metaobject, you edit one entry, and it updates everywhere it’s referenced.
Author bios, testimonials, or FAQ sets that show up on multiple pages — homepage, collection pages, landing pages, all from a single source.

A size guide used across 80 products. Store locations appearing in a footer, a map page, and a contact block simultaneously. A recipe content type, with fields for prep time, ingredients, and steps, that isn’t a product at all but needs its own structure.
Is this data reused across multiple resources, or is it unique to just one? If it’s shared, lean toward a metaobject.

Does the data have real internal structure, multiple sub-fields, related images, typed values? Even for a single use case, that structure often makes a metaobject cleaner to manage than a single metafield.

contentAfterToc.text: What Goes Wrong When You Choose Wrong

content: A “brand story” metafield copied across 200 products means 200 separate edits every time the story changes.
Creating a standalone metaobject for a value that only ever appears in one place adds complexity and API overhead with no real benefit.

children: If it’s unique to one resource, use a metafield. If it’s shared, reused, or has real structure of its own, use a metaobject. Getting this right early saves significant rework later, especially for stores with large catalogs or complex content needs.
